chunks: From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Dirraj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding a man who eats at the place of his creditor, or drinks from his drink, or is gifted a present by him, he said: 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.غَرِيمِهِ: his creditor (one to whom money is owed)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm in it (permissible)

ai.seo_question: Does a gift from a creditor to a debtor invalidate the debt or count as usury?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify that casual hospitality or gifts between debtor and creditor do not constitute *riba al-fadl* or invalidate the principal debt, provided no explicit condition is attached. This distinction is crucial in Shia jurisprudence for distinguishing between social courtesy and contractual usury, ensuring that everyday interactions do not complicate debt settlements. The narration underscores the flexibility of commercial ethics in Islam, allowing for generosity without altering the legal standing of the loan.
